newsitem.title: USA: N.J. voters want Yankees to stay in N.Y. - survey.
newsitem.headline: N.J. voters want Yankees to stay in N.Y. - survey.

text.p: New Jersey voters want to keep the Yankees baseball team, which wants its historic Bronx stadium renovated or a new one built at another site, in New York by a 48 to 27 percent margin, a survey said on Thursday.
And the Quinnipiac College Poll said New Jersey voters who were surveyed by a 50 to 30 percent margin want to keep the World Series Champions in the Bronx.

However, when the 874 New Jersey residents, who said they were registered voters and were polled from December 2 to 9, were asked where they would most likely go to see a Yankees home game, 64 percent chose the Meadowlands in northern New Jersey, where two professional football teams play.

Only nine percent selected the Yankees' Bronx stadium, and only a slim four percent chose a new stadium on Manhattan's West Side, a project estimated to cost around $1 billion that now is being studied.
A total of 17 percent of those polled said the site did not matter, while seven percent were undecided.

Most New Jersey voters want the Yankees to pay for building a new stadium in their state, if that option is the one selected by the team, as 55 percent of those surveyed said the team should pick up the tab. Only six percent said the state should pay, while 30 percent said an independent authority in the Meadowlands should pay.
On a statewide basis, 40 percent of New Jersey's voters call themselves Yankees fans, with a bigger portion of northern New Jersey's residents, 51 percent, putting themselves in that category.

"New Jersey voters won't put out the welcome mat for the Yankees. While we know that South Jersey residents tend to be Philadelphia Phillies fans, the North Jersey voters tend to follow the Yankees. Even among these North Jersey voters, the message is: Yankees, stay home," said Maurice Carroll, director of the Quinnipiac College Polling Institute, in prepared remarks.
The poll's margin of error was plus or minus 3.3 percent.
